# Introduction {#sec-introduction}


# Derivative and differentiability


::: {.callout-note title="Derivative and differentiability"}

::: {#def-derivative}

Consider the function $f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ and a [**accumulation point**](0_sets_and_functions.qmd#def-accumulation-point)  $x_{0}\in D$.

Define the set of admissible increments
$$
H_{x_{0}}:=\{h\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\,:\,x_{0}+h\in D\},
$$
and the function $\Delta f\colon H_{x_{0}}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by
$$
\Delta f(h):=\frac{f(x_{0}+h) - f(x_{0})}{h} .
$$
If the limit 
$$
\lim_{\substack{h\rightarrow 0 \\ h\in H_{x_{0}}}}\Delta f(h)= l
$$
exists with $l\in\mathbb{R}$, we say that $l$ is the derivative of $f$ at $x_{0}$, and that $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$. 

When $f$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$, we write
$$
f'(x_{0})\equiv \lim_{\substack{h\rightarrow 0 \\ h\in H_{x_{0}}}}\Delta f(h)=\lim_{\substack{h\rightarrow 0 \\ h\in H_{x_{0}}}}\frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}.
$$
We also write 
$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d} x}(x_{0})\equiv f'(x_{0}),
$$
and refer to this expression as the _Leibniz_ notation for derivatives.

If $f$ is differentiable at all $x\in D$, we say that $f$ is differentiable in $D$.


The function determined by the rule $x\mapsto f'(x)$ (whenever it makes sense) is called the **derivative** of $f$.  Its domain **need not** coincide with the domain of $f$.
:::

:::

Before we learn some useful tricks that make computing (a lot but not all) derivatives a sort of mechanical task that does not require computing limits, let's work out some derivatives from the very definition.

::: {.callout-tip title="Derivative of constant functions"}

::: {#exm-derivative-constant-functions}

The first example of derivative we consider is that of a constant function $f(x)=c$ with $c\in \mathbb{R}$. Following the very definition of  derivative given above, we have
$$
f'(x_{0})=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}=0
$$
for every $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$. 

:::

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Derivative of linear functions"}

::: {#exm-derivative-linear-functions}

The second example we consider is that of the linear function $f(x)=ax$ with $a\in\mathbb{R}$:
$$
f'(x_{0})=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{a(x_{0} + h) -ax_{0}}{h}=a
$$
for every $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$.

:::

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Derivative of quadratic functions"}

::: {#exm-derivative-quadratic-functions}

The third example we consider is that of the function $f(x)=ax^{2}$:
$$
\begin{split}
f'(x_{0})&=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x_{0}+h)-f(x_{0})}{h}= \\ &=\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{a(x_{0} + h)^{2} -ax_{0}^{2}}{h}= \\ &\lim_{h\rightarrow 0} \frac{2ax_{0}h + ah^{2}}{h}=2ax_{0}
\end{split}
$$
for every $x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}$.


:::

:::

We defined the derivative of $f$ at $x_{0}$ assuming $x_{0}$ is an accumulation point. However, we can also relax this assumption to the case where $x_{0}$ is either a left or right accumulation point, obtaining the notions of left/right derivative and differentiability. 



::: {.callout-caution title="Right and left derivative"}

::: {#exr-left-right-derivative}

Consider the function $f\colon D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.

If $x_{0}\in D$ is a left or right accumulation point, define the right or left derivative and differentiability of $f$ at $x_{0}$ using [left/right limits](1_limits_and_continuity.qmd#def-limits), and prove that, when $x_{0}$ is both a left **and** right accumulation point, the differentiability of $f$ at $x_{0}$ is equivalent to left **and** right differentiability.

<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>

You are strongly invited to try to solve it on your own.
</details>

:::

:::

Just as it happens for [limits](1_limits_and_continuity.qmd#exr-limits-restriction-functions), derivatives behave well with respect to restrictions.

::: {.callout-caution title="Derivative of the restriction"}

::: {#exr-derivative-restriction-functions}

Consider $D,D'\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $D\cap D'\neq \emptyset$, and consider two functions $f\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $g\colon D' \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that both are differentiable at $x_{0}\in D\cap D'$.
Assume there is a subset $S\subseteq D\cap D'$ such that $x_{0}$ is an accumulation point for $S$ and $g(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in S$.
Prove that
$$
f'(x_{0})=g'(x_{0}),
$$
and prove analogous results for the case of left and right derivatives.

<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>

**TBA**
</details>

:::

:::


Once a definition is in place, it's always a good idea to go searching for situations in which the definition itself can not be applied.

::: {.callout-tip title="Absolute value function is not differentiable at $x=0$"}

::: {#exm-abs-value-function-not-diff-at-0}

Let us consider the absolute value function $|\cdot|\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ given by 
$$
|x|=\sqrt{x^{2}}=\left\{\begin{matrix}x & \mbox{ if } x\geq 0 \\ & \\ -x & \mbox{ if } x<0 .\end{matrix}\right.
$$
For all points $x_{0}\neq 0$, we can compute the derivative following @exm-derivative-linear-functions (essentially because of @exr-derivative-restriction-functions). However, when $x_{0}=0$, we have to take into account the "sudden change" of the function. Therefore, we first compute the [right and left derivatives](#exr-left-right-derivative): 
$$
\begin{split}
\lim_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{x-0}{x}&=1 \\ & \\
\lim_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{-x-0}{x}&=-1 .
\end{split}
$$
Since the two derivatives exist but are different, we conclude that $|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$ (but it is separately left and right differentiable there).

:::

:::

# Properties of derivatives

The first "property" of derivatives we want to highlight is that it requires continuity.

::: {.callout-note title="Differentiability implies continuity"}

::: {#prp-diff-implies-cont}

If the function $f\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is (left/right) differentiable at $x_{0}\in D$, then it is also (left/right) continuous at $x_{0}$. 

<details>
<summary>**Proof:**</summary>

You are strongly invited to try to prove it on your own.
</details>

:::

:::

Note, however, that the converse of the previous proposition does not hold. An explicit counterexample is given by the absolute value function in @exm-abs-value-function-not-diff-at-0.


Next, we pass to how derivatives behave with respect to sums and products of 2 functions.

::: {.callout-note title="Algebraic manipulations of derivatives"}

::: {#prp-algebraic-manipulations-derivatives}

Given $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ and the functions $f,g\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ differentiable at $x_{0}\in D$, the functions $h,r\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ given by $h:=\alpha f+\beta g$ and $r:=f\cdot g$ are differentiable at $x_{0}$ and their derivatives are
$$
\begin{split}
h'(x_{0})&=\alpha f'(x_{0}) + \beta g'(x_{0}),\\
r'(x_{0})& =f'(x_{0})\,g(x_{0}) + f(x_{0})\,g'(x_{0}).
\end{split}
$$
The formula for the derivative of the product of two functions is usually referred to as the **Leibniz rule**.

<details>
<summary>**Proof:**</summary>

**TBA**
</details>

:::

:::


What happens when we have more than 2 functions? For a small number of functions, say between 3 and 7, it should be not extremely boring to use the associativity property of function sums and products to understand how to generalize @prp-algebraic-manipulations-derivatives. For an arbitrary finite number of functions, the generalization can be obtained using the induction principle.

::: {.callout-caution title="Algebraic manipulations of derivatives continued"}

::: {#exr-algebraic-manipulations-derivatives-N-functions}

Let $(\alpha_{1},\cdots\alpha_{n})$ be a finite sequence of real numbers and $(f_{1},\cdots,f_{n})$ a finite sequence of scalar functions with common domain $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Suppose that, at $x_{0}\in D$, the derivatives $f_{j}'(x_{0})$ exist for every $j=1,...,n$. Then, it holds
$$
\begin{split}
\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}\right)'(x_{0}) &=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\, \alpha_{j}\,f_{j}'(x_{0})  \\
\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n} \,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}\right)'(x_{0}) &=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}'(x_{0})\,\left(\prod_{k\neq j}\alpha_{k}\,f_{k}(x_{0})\right).
\end{split}
$$

<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>

Fix an accumulation point $x_0\in D$ and assume that $f_j'(x_0)$ exists for all $j=1,\dots,n$.
Set $g_j:=\alpha_j f_j$, so that $g_j'(x_0)=\alpha_j f_j'(x_0)$.

We will use the two-function rules from @prp-algebraic-manipulations-derivatives

---

We start with the derivative of the sum of finitely many functions.


For $h\neq 0$ with $x_0+h\in D$, we have
$$
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j(x_0+h)-\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j(x_0)}{h}
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \frac{f_j(x_0+h)-f_j(x_0)}{h}.
$$
Following @def-derivative, we take the limit as $h\to 0$:
$$
\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\,\alpha_{j}\,f_{j}\right)'(x_{0}) 
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f_j(x_0+h)-f_j(x_0)}{h}
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j'(x_0),
$$
where we passed the limit through the sum because it's a sum of finitely many elements.

---

Now, we pass to the derivative of the product of finitely many functions.

Define
$$
P_n(x):=\prod_{j=1}^n g_j(x).
$$

**Base case ($n=1$):** $P_1=g_1$, hence
$$
P_1'(x_0)=g_1'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^1 g_j'(x_0)\prod_{k\neq j} g_k(x_0),
$$
so the formula holds.

**Inductive step:** assume that for some $n\ge 1$,
$$
P_n'(x_0)=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^n g_k(x_0).
$$
Now $P_{n+1}=P_n\,g_{n+1}$. By the two-function product rule,
$$
P_{n+1}'(x_0)=P_n'(x_0)\,g_{n+1}(x_0)+P_n(x_0)\,g_{n+1}'(x_0).
$$
Substitute the inductive hypothesis into the first term:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{n+1}'(x_0)
&=\left(\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^n g_k(x_0)\right) g_{n+1}(x_0)
+ \left(\prod_{k=1}^n g_k(x_0)\right) g_{n+1}'(x_0)\\[4pt]
&=\sum_{j=1}^n g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^{n+1} g_k(x_0)
\;+\; g_{n+1}'(x_0)\prod_{k=1}^n g_k(x_0)\\[4pt]
&=\sum_{j=1}^{n+1} g_j'(x_0)\prod_{\substack{k=1\\k\neq j}}^{n+1} g_k(x_0).
\end{aligned}
$$
Finally, replacing $g_j=\alpha_j f_j$ and $g_j'(x_0)=\alpha_j f_j'(x_0)$, we obtain
$$
\left(\prod_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j\right)'(x_0)
=\sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j f_j'(x_0)\left(\prod_{k\neq j}\alpha_k f_k(x_0)\right).
$$

This concludes the proof.
</details>


:::

:::


::: {.callout-caution title="A foundational example"}

 
 
::: {#exr-derivative-monomial}

Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Prove that  the derivative of the function $f_{n}\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ given by $f_{n}(x)=\alpha_{n}x^{n}$  with $\alpha_{n}\in \mathbb{R}$ is $n\alpha_{n}x^{n-1}$.



<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>

Use @exm-derivative-linear-functions together with @exr-algebraic-manipulations-derivatives-N-functions.
 

</details>

:::

:::





Now, we consider what happens to the derivative of the quotient of two functions.

::: {.callout-note title="Derivative of the quotient"}

::: {#prp-derivative-quotient}

Given the functions $f,g\colon D\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ differentiable at $x_{0}\in D$ and with $g(x_{0})\neq 0$, define
$$
\tilde{D}:=\{x\in D \,:\, g(x)\neq 0\},
$$
and the function $h\colon \tilde{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ given by $h:=\frac{f}{g}$.
Then $h$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$ and its derivative is
$$
h'(x_{0})= \frac{f'(x_{0})\,g(x_{0})-f(x_{0})\,g'(x_{0})}{(g(x_{0}))^{2}}.
$$

<details>
<summary>**Proof:**</summary>

**TBA**
</details>

:::

:::

Finally, we are able to use all the results presented in this section to compute the derivatives of polynomial and rational functions without ever computing a limit.

::: {.callout-caution title="Derivatives of polynomials and rational functions"}

 
 
::: {#exr-derivative-polynomial-rational-functions}



Let $P_{n},Q_{m}\colon \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be polynomial functions.
Compute $P_{n}',Q_{m}'$, and $R'$, where $R=\frac{P_{n}}{Q_{m}}$ is defined on the maximal domain $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ on which $Q_{m}(x)\neq 0$.



<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>



To compute the derivative of $P_{n}$, we first write
$$
P_{n}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\alpha_{k}\,x^{k}
$$
with $\alpha_{k}\in\mathbb{R}$, and then  use @exr-algebraic-manipulations-derivatives-N-functions together with @exr-derivative-monomial to conclude that the derivative $P_{n}'$ of $P_{n}$ is the polynomial of order $(n-1)$ given by
$$
P_{n}'(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\alpha_{k}\,x^{k-1}.
$$
A similar result holds for $Q_{m}'(x)$.

The derivative of $R(x)=\frac{P_{n}(x)}{Q_{m}(x)}$ can then be immediately obtained using the previous results and @prp-derivative-quotient:

$$
R'(x)=\frac{P'_{n}(x)Q_{m}(x) - P_{n}(x)Q'_{m}(x)}{(Q_{m}(x))^{2}}.
$$
</details>

:::

:::

# Derivative of inverse and composite functions

In [composition of continuous functions](1_limits_and_continuity.qmd#prp-composition-continuous-functions) and [continuity of inverse function](1_limits_and_continuity.qmd#prp-continuity-inverse-function), we saw that continuity behaves well under composition and inversion on intervals. We now ask the analogous question for differentiability, and the answer is again positive under suitable hypotheses.

::: {.callout-note title="Chain rule"}

::: {#prp-chain-rule}

Consider the functions $f\colon D\subseteq \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $g\colon D'\subseteq \mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, and assume that $g(D')\subseteq D$.
If $g$ is differentiable at $x_{0}\in D'$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(x_{0})\in D$, then the composite function $r:=f\circ g$ is differentiable at $x_{0}$ and
$$
r'(x_{0})=(f\circ g)'(x_{0})=f'(g(x_{0}))\,g'(x_{0}).
$$

<details>
<summary>**Proof:**</summary>

Define the auxiliary function $\phi\colon D\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by
$$
\phi(y):=
\left\{
\begin{matrix}
\dfrac{f(y)-f(g(x_{0}))}{y-g(x_{0})} & \mbox{ if } y\neq g(x_{0}), \\ & \\
f'(g(x_{0})) & \mbox{ if } y=g(x_{0}) .
\end{matrix}
\right.
$$
Since $f$ is differentiable at $g(x_{0})$, it follows from @def-derivative that
$$
\lim_{y\rightarrow g(x_{0})}\phi(y)=f'(g(x_{0})),
$$
so $\phi$ is continuous at $g(x_{0})$.

Moreover, @prp-diff-implies-cont implies that $g$ is continuous at $x_{0}$, that is,
$$
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}g(x)=g(x_{0}).
$$
Since $\phi$ is continuous at $g(x_{0})$, [limit of composite functions](1_limits_and_continuity.qmd#prp-limit-composite-functions) implies that
$$
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}} \phi(g(x))=\phi(g(x_{0}))=f'(g(x_{0})).
$$

For every $h\neq 0$ such that $x_{0}+h\in D'$, we have
$$
\frac{r(x_{0}+h)-r(x_{0})}{h}
=\frac{f(g(x_{0}+h))-f(g(x_{0}))}{h}
=\phi(g(x_{0}+h))\,\frac{g(x_{0}+h)-g(x_{0})}{h}.
$$
Indeed, if $g(x_{0}+h)\neq g(x_{0})$, the identity follows from the definition of $\phi$, while if $g(x_{0}+h)= g(x_{0})$, both sides are equal to $0$.

Passing to the limit as $h\to 0$, we obtain
$$
\begin{split}
r'(x_{0})
&=\lim_{h\to 0}\phi(g(x_{0}+h))\,\frac{g(x_{0}+h)-g(x_{0})}{h} \\
&=\left(\lim_{h\to 0}\phi(g(x_{0}+h))\right)\left(\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{g(x_{0}+h)-g(x_{0})}{h}\right) \\
&=f'(g(x_{0}))\,g'(x_{0}),
\end{split}
$$
as claimed.
</details>

:::

:::

::: {.callout-caution title="A first exercise on the chain rule"}

::: {#exr-chain-rule-polynomial}

Compute the derivative of the function
$$
f(x)=\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{3}.
$$

<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>

Define
$$
g(x):=x^{2}+1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
h(y):=y^{3},
$$
so that $f=h\circ g$.

From @exm-derivative-quadratic-functions, @exm-derivative-constant-functions, and @prp-algebraic-manipulations-derivatives, we obtain
$$
g'(x)=2x.
$$
From @exr-derivative-monomial, we know that
$$
h'(y)=3y^{2}.
$$
Applying @prp-chain-rule, we conclude that
$$
f'(x)=h'(g(x))\,g'(x)=3(x^{2}+1)^{2}\cdot 2x=6x(x^{2}+1)^{2}.
$$
</details>

:::

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Derivative of inverse functions"}

::: {#prp-derivative-inverse-function}

Let $I$ be an interval, let $f\colon I\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable and invertible on $I$, and set $J:=f(I)$.
Fix $x_{0}\in I$ and write $y_{0}:=f(x_{0})$.
If $f'(x_{0})\neq 0$, then the inverse function $f^{-1}\colon J\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is differentiable at $y_{0}$ and
$$
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(y_{0})=\frac{1}{f'(x_{0})}.
$$

<details>
<summary>**Proof:**</summary>

Since $f$ is differentiable on $I$, @prp-diff-implies-cont implies that $f$ is continuous on $I$.
Therefore, [continuity of inverse function](1_limits_and_continuity.qmd#prp-continuity-inverse-function) guarantees that $f^{-1}$ is continuous on $J$.

Take $y\in J$ with $y\neq y_{0}$, and set $x:=f^{-1}(y)$.
Then $x\neq x_{0}$ because $f$ is invertible, and $y=f(x)$.
Hence
$$
\frac{f^{-1}(y)-f^{-1}(y_{0})}{y-y_{0}}
=\frac{x-x_{0}}{f(x)-f(x_{0})}
=\left(\frac{f(x)-f(x_{0})}{x-x_{0}}\right)^{-1}.
$$

Now let $y\rightarrow y_{0}$ in $J$.
Since $f^{-1}$ is continuous at $y_{0}$ by [continuity of inverse function](1_limits_and_continuity.qmd#prp-continuity-inverse-function), we have
$$
x=f^{-1}(y)\rightarrow f^{-1}(y_{0})=x_{0}.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\begin{split}
\left(f^{-1}\right)'(y_{0})
&=\lim_{y\rightarrow y_{0}}\frac{f^{-1}(y)-f^{-1}(y_{0})}{y-y_{0}} \\
&=\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}\left(\frac{f(x)-f(x_{0})}{x-x_{0}}\right)^{-1} \\
&=\left(\lim_{x\rightarrow x_{0}}\frac{f(x)-f(x_{0})}{x-x_{0}}\right)^{-1} \\
&=\frac{1}{f'(x_{0})},
\end{split}
$$
where the reciprocal is legitimate because $f'(x_{0})\neq 0$.
</details>

:::

:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Derivative of root functions"}

::: {#exr-derivative-root-functions}

Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$ with $n\geq 1$, and let $D$ be the maximal domain on which the function
$$
p_{n}(x)=x^{n}
$$
admits an inverse. Explicitly, $D=\mathbb{R}$ if $n$ is odd and $D=\mathbb{R}_{+}$ if $n$ is even.
Use @prp-derivative-inverse-function to compute the derivative of
$$
g(y)=y^{\frac{1}{n}}=p_{n}^{-1}(y)
$$
at points $y_{0}\in p_{n}(D)$ for which the proposition applies.

<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>

Fix $y_{0}\in p_{n}(D)$ and set $x_{0}:=g(y_{0})=y_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}}$.
By @exr-derivative-monomial, the derivative of $p_{n}$ is
$$
p_{n}'(x)=nx^{n-1}.
$$
Therefore, if $x_{0}\neq 0$, then
$$
p_{n}'(x_{0})=n x_{0}^{n-1}\neq 0,
$$
and @prp-derivative-inverse-function yields
$$
g'(y_{0})=\frac{1}{p_{n}'(x_{0})}
=\frac{1}{n x_{0}^{n-1}}
=\frac{1}{n\left(y_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}}\right)^{n-1}}
=\frac{1}{n}y_{0}^{\frac{1}{n}-1}.
$$

If $n>1$ and $y_{0}=0$, then $x_{0}=0$ and
$$
p_{n}'(0)=0,
$$
so @prp-derivative-inverse-function does not apply. Therefore, for $n>1$, the derivative formula above is valid only at points $y_{0}\neq 0$.
</details>

:::

:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Right derivative at the origin for even roots"}

::: {#exr-right-derivative-even-root-functions}

Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$ be even and satisfy $n\geq 2$.
Consider the function $g\colon \mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ given by
$$
g(y)=y^{\frac{1}{n}}.
$$
Study the right derivative of $g$ at $0$.

<details>
<summary> **Solution:** </summary>

Since $g(0)=0$, for every $h>0$ we have
$$
\frac{g(0+h)-g(0)}{h}
=\frac{h^{\frac{1}{n}}}{h}
=h^{\frac{1}{n}-1}
=h^{-\frac{n-1}{n}}.
$$
Because $-\frac{n-1}{n}<0$, the previous quantity tends to $+\infty$ as $h\rightarrow 0^{+}$.

Therefore, $g$ does not admit a finite right derivative at $0$.
Equivalently, the right difference quotient has unbounded limit $+\infty$ at the origin.
</details>

:::

:::

Together, the chain rule and the derivative of inverse functions will allow us to compute derivatives of rational powers and much more complicated compositions without returning to the definition every time.
